                                    PROJECT NO. 58481
 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                    §                  OF TEXAS


              TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS’ COMMENTS

                                    I.    INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) appreciates Commission Staff’s (Staff’s)
continued efforts to incorporate stakeholder feedback into this rulemaking. This rulemaking has
presented significant complexities with numerous moving parts and a wide range of perspectives
among stakeholders. TIEC appreciates Staff’s thorough and methodical approach in developing
multiple Discussion Drafts, soliciting stakeholder feedback, and hosting workshops to ensure that
this rulemaking—and related initiatives—are coordinated and provide practical solutions to
concerns regarding large load interconnections.

       In further support of Staff’s efforts, TIEC submits additional comments following the
Workshop held on January 9th. Our intent is to help capture stakeholder feedback and ensure the
development of a balanced framework—one that discourages speculative load forecasts without
relying exclusively on a “pay to play” mechanism to determine the legitimacy or viability of
proposed projects. TIEC recommends additional refinements to the updated Discussion Draft and
offers specific suggested language where appropriate below.

            II.    COMMENTS ON STAFF’S SECOND DISCUSSION DRAFT

A.     The Commission should remove the proposed language that would give ERCOT carte
       blanche authority to impose operational requirements on large loads.
       As discussed in TIEC’s initial comments, § 25.194(m) of Staff’s Second Discussion Draft
adds controversial language allowing ERCOT to establish registration and operational standards
for large load customers and requiring large load customers to comply with ERCOT’s standards
as a condition for interconnection and continued operations. This is outside the scope of SB 6,
legally controversial, and poor public policy.        The SB 6 rulemaking process needs to be
expeditiously completed, so at a minimum, this issue should be addressed in a separate, dedicated
rulemaking to consider appropriate standards and limitations for this authority. A separate


                                                  1
 rulemaking would allow for a more robust legal analysis and provide a greater opportunity for
entities to engage in the discussion to help the Commission and ERCOT fully consider potential
implications and alternative solutions. TIEC sees no reason to attach this controversial issue to
the SB 6 implementation.

       However, TIEC understands that part of ERCOT’s goal with this proposed language is to
ensure compliance with PURA § 37.0561(e), which requires customers with on-site backup
generation sufficient to serve at least 50% of their load to curtail in advance of firm load shed.
TIEC reads the following provisions of the statute as requiring the customer’s utility to administer
these requirements, and not ERCOT:

               “The [large load] standards must require each interconnected large
               load customer subject to Subsection (c) to disclose to the
               interconnecting electric utility or municipally owned utility
               information about the customer’s on-site backup generating
               facilities and require the interconnecting electric utility or
               municipally owned utility to provide the information to the
               independent organization certified under Section 39.151 for the
               ERCOT power region.”
               ...
               “the independent organization may direct the applicable electric
               utility or municipally owned utility to require the large load customer
               to either deploy the customer’s on-site backup generating facilities
               or curtail load.”

That being said, TIEC appreciates that ERCOT may need to understand in real-time what capacity
is being made available through these deployments for their own operational purposes. TIEC
would be open to including a rule provision that would allow ERCOT to have access to contact
information for sites with backup generation and potentially additional telemetry or other
communication equipment as needed for emergency operations. As a starting point TIEC suggests
the following as a potential replacement for subsection (m):

       (m)     Backup Generating Facilities. ERCOT may establish informational requirements
               for electric utilities, electric cooperatives and municipally owned utilities serving a
               large load customer with on-site backup generating facilities. These requirements
               may include sharing a customer point of contact with ERCOT, installing additional
               telemetry or communications equipment, or providing other customer information


                                                 2
                as needed to facilitate ERCOT real-time operations during an emergency.

       TIEC also understands that ERCOT is likely to develop a portal to allow large load
customers to view their project status during interconnection, which TIEC strongly supports.
Similar to other features of the ERCOT website that require secure access, TIEC has no concerns
with ERCOT imposing a registration or attestation requirement on customers solely for the purpose
of validating identities and ensuring secure access to this type of portal, if the customer desires
access. TIEC does not believe this needs to be addressed in the rule as this is within ERCOT’s
existing authority and is similar to registration requirements that already exist today for digital
users. TIEC maintains its concerns regarding any other operational or registration requirements
for pure retail customers as set forth in initial comments.

B.     The CIAC and financial security obligations should be refined to ensure appropriate
       cost assignment of customer-dedicated versus grid-dedicated facilities.
       Consistent with stakeholder feedback at the Workshop, the CIAC language should be
adjusted to capture costs that are incurred solely to serve a large load customer, and system costs
should not be part of the CIAC payment. As currently drafted, the description of the CIAC requires
large customers to pay for facilities that will be used to serve other customers and the grid at large.
Specifically, the language in subsection (i)(9) references the costs associated with system upgrades
that would not exist “but for” the interconnecting large load customer. As highlighted in more
detail in TIEC’s initial comments and by numerous parties at the Workshop, this standard does not
work. System upgrades are needed to serve total load—including the new customer and all
existing customers. Both the new customer and all existing customers are the “but for” cause of
the improvements, so it is not clear how the Commission will identify when an improvement would
be needed “but for” the interconnecting large load. For example, which customer(s) were the “but
for” cause of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan? Similarly, identifying which customer causes a
system improvement will only become more difficult when ERCOT implements its batching study
process for large loads, which will study multiple large loads simultaneously. If a batch of fifteen
large loads requires a certain amount of upgrades, ERCOT would have to take out each large load
individually to try to figure out which upgrade is associated with a specific customer. The utilities
also described at the Workshop how this approach is at odds with contingency planning. The “but
for” cause of most transmission upgrades is overloads on other elements under a contingency


                                                  3
 analysis when trying to serve total load. As such, it would be resource intensive, if not practically
impossible, to isolate the portion of a system upgrade actually caused by each specific customer.

       If the concern is ensuring that new large load customers appropriately contribute to system
costs, this is better handled in Project No. 58484. As noted at the workshop, TIEC believes an
approach like establishing a minimum charge for new large load customers for some defined
period of time would preserve cost-causation for wholesale TCOS while ensuring that customers
causing upgrades cannot avoid paying transmission costs. The Commission could consider a
minimum demand charge for particularly large loads who are likely to justify significant
transmission upgrades (for example, greater than 200 MW) for a limited period to ensure that the
loads are paying for transmission. At the workshop TIEC suggested five years, with the reasoning
that after five years overall load will typically “grow into” any system upgrades and this type of
protection is no longer needed. Further, after five years of operational experience the load’s
behavior during peak demand conditions can be evaluated and factored into planning. This type
of a construct or other alternatives that protect ratepayers from stranded transmission costs could
be considered in more detail in Project No. 58484.

       Additionally, the Commission should give large loads flexibility in meeting their CIAC
obligations with cash, corporate or parental guarantees, or letters of credit. Notably, Staff’s Second
Discussion Draft removed alternative forms of CIAC payments, so the rule only allows large loads
to meet their CIAC obligation through cash payments. A letter of credit or a corporate or parental
guarantee protects ratepayers and utilities from stranded investments, similar to cash. Frequently
it can take many years before construction starts on CIAC facilities, so there is no need to tie up
tens of millions of dollars in cash before the utility incurs any costs. As such, allowing options
such as corporate or parental guarantees or letters of credit provides utilities with protection while
giving large loads additional flexibility.

       To address the issues outlined above, the Discussion Draft § (i)(9) should be amended as
follows:

               (9)     Contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). An interconnecting utility
                       must not begin construction of facilities to interconnect a large load
                       customer before a large load customer pays a CIAC fee in an amount that
                       is equal to the interconnecting utility’s estimated costs to interconnect the

                                                  4
 large load customer and that is directly solely attributable to interconnecting
the large load customer. The CIAC must be trued-up to reflect the
interconnecting utility’s actual costs once the facilities are completed, and
a customer may receive a surcharge or refund for the difference in actual
costs relative to the estimate.

(A)     Costs directly solely attributable to interconnecting the large load
        customer include all costs associated with transmission facilities
        built to interconnect the large load customer to the existing
        transmission network, including substation upgrades associated
        with interconnecting the new large load customer, where such
        facilities are not anticipated to serve other customers in the near
        term. CIAC must be paid in the form of a direct cash payment.

(B)     Costs associated with system upgrades that are reasonably
        anticipated to serve other customers in the near term would not be
        required but for the interconnecting large load customer are not costs
        directly solely attributable to the interconnecting large load
        customer. Where a system upgrade is necessary to serve multiple
        large load customers, such system upgrade costs must be pro-rated
        among those large load customers based on the contracted peak
        demand of each of those customers.

(C)     For a large load customer that is interconnecting to an existing
        transmission    asset,    costs   directly   solely   attributable   to
        interconnecting the large load customer include a share of any the
        original CIAC that another large load customer paid under this
        section. The share of original CIAC must be calculated based on
        remaining net book value of the associated costs as a fraction of the
        original book value of those costs, and further pro-rated based on
        the share of contracted peak demand all large load customers
        associated with that transmission asset, including the new large load


                           5
                               customer. CIAC payments under this subsection must be credited to
                              the previous large load customers that contributed to the previous
                              CIAC payments, on an asset by asset basis, in proportion to those
                              previous payments.

                      (D)     The interconnecting electric utility may accept the following forms
                              of payment for CIAC:

                              (i)     cash collateral;

                              (ii)    corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or
                                      parent corporation has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-
                                      /Baa3 or higher from Standard & Poor’s or Moody’s; or

                              (iii)   a letter of credit issued by a U.S. commercial bank, or a U.S.
                                      branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a
                                      credit rating of at least “A-” by Standard & Poor’s or “A3”
                                      by Moody’s Investor Service.

                      (E)     If the large load customer provides a corporate or parental guaranty
                              under this subsection, the interconnecting utility may require
                              submission of financial records or statements to determine the
                              customer’s financial stability.

C.     The generic intermediate security amount should be reduced and should take into
       account any security provided for significant equipment or services procured prior
       to executing an interconnection agreement.
       Under the Second Discussion Draft, the $/MW security associated with the Intermediate
Agreement is $100,000/MW, which is significantly higher than typical security and CIAC
requirements in a final service agreement. This level of a security requirement, even if it is
ultimately refunded, may deter desirable and legitimate economic activity—particularly from cost-
sensitive industrial businesses competing in global markets. While this security will only be held
until a final service agreement is executed, that process can take a year or more today, and it is
uncertain what the process will look like if “batching” is implemented. The $/MW security is


                                                 6
 meant to act as a proxy for the costs of a final service agreement to determine whether a load is
“real” during the study process. As CenterPoint highlighted during the Workshop, applying the
$100,000/MW security requirement to a 2.5 GW customer load it is studying would amount to
$250 million—far exceeding the actual interconnection costs, which CenterPoint estimated to be
in the tens of millions. 1 This demonstrates that such a high upfront generic security amount not
only unnecessarily ties up a large load customer’s capital/credit, but also does little to verify the
legitimacy of the proposed load. In light of stakeholder feedback, TIEC recommends reducing the
security requirement to $20,000/MW to better reflect the actual purpose of the security amount.
For a large load, this amount would still be at least $1.5 million for a 75 MW load, instead of the
Second Discussion Draft’s $7.5 million.

        Alternatively, TIEC re-urges its prior suggestion to adopt a tiered $/MW security amount
based on load size, similar to the distinction for the large load study fee. For example, a large load
customer with requested peak demand that is equal to 75 MW and less than 250 MW would be
subject to a $20,000/MW security requirement, while a large load customer with requested peak
demand that is equal to or greater than 250 MW would be required to pay $50,000/MW. Both
tiers provide sufficient security to ensure that the load is legitimate and committed, while also
aligning more closely with actual costs. This approach ensures that the security requirement is
proportionate to the scale of the load, promoting fairness and still protecting ratepayers and system
reliability.

        In addition, the $/MW security should recognize that a utility may request security for
certain long-lead time equipment prior to executing an interconnection agreement, and any security
provided for such equipment should count towards the $/MW requirement. Notably, the current
language in the Second Discussion Draft gives utilities flexibility to securitize long-lead time
equipment at any stage of the of the interconnection process. Critically, Staff’s Second Discussion
Draft only requires utilities to obtain financial security for any significant equipment or services
once an interconnection agreement is signed. However, there is nothing to prohibit a utility from
executing a Discretionary Services Agreement (DSA) or some other interim agreement and



        1

Under PURA 37.0561 at 2:14:41-2:15:25 (January 9, 2026) (available at:
https://dash2.gridmonitor.com/sharing/?token=*** .


                                                      7
 collecting security earlier in the interconnection process. This is consistent with many utilities’
current practices. As CenterPoint explained, it uses an interim agreement in order to work on the
transmission interconnection facilities as early as possible before even completing studies. 2 Auto
transformers, transmission breaker bays, and other long-lead time equipment must be ordered well
in advance and are known to be necessary even before an Interconnection Agreement is executed. 3
Unlike the generic $/MW security, security for significant equipment is based on estimates of the
actual costs of any required facilities. Maintaining a security in excess of the $/MW amount
(unless it is associated with the actual cost of any facilities) provides no significant benefit to
utilities or their ratepayers. As such, the Second Discussion Draft needs to be adjusted to make it
clear that any additional security provided before executing an interconnection agreement counts
against the $/MW security requirement. If the security for long-lead time equipment is greater
than the generic security amount, then no $/MW security should be required.

        To address the issues outlined above including the alternative $/MW suggestion, the
Second Discussion Draft § (f)(8) should be amended as follows:

                 (8)     Financial security on a dollar per MW basis. A large load customer must
                         pay financial security to the interconnecting utility in the amount of
                         $100,000 per MW of the contracted peak demand for new interconnection
                         requests or of the incremental increase in the peak demand for expanded
                         interconnection requests. The financial security amounts set forth below
                         shall be reduced by the amount of security provided for any equipment or
                         services procured prior to executing an interconnection agreement.

                         (A)      A large load customer with requested peak demand that is equal to
                                  75 MW and less than 250 MW must pay financial security to the
                                  interconnecting     electric    utility   of   $20,000/MW         for     new
                                  interconnection requests or the incremental increase in the peak


        2

Under PURA 37.0561 at 2:28:39-2:29:05 (January 9, 2026) (available at:
https://dash2.gridmonitor.com/sharing/?token=***        3

Under PURA 37.0561 at 2:26:45-2:27:29 (available at: https://dash2.gridmonitor.com/sharing/?token=***                                                      8
                                   demand for expanded interconnection requests.

                         (B)      A large load customer with requested peak demand that is equal to
                                  or greater than 250 MW must pay financial security to the
                                  interconnecting       electric   utility   of   $50,000/MW   for   new
                                  interconnection requests or the incremental increase in the peak
                                  demand for expanded interconnection requests.

                         (C)      Beginning in 2027, the commission will adjust the $100,000
                                  $20,000 and $50,000 values on January 1 of each calendar year.

                                  (i)     The annual adjustment will be proportional to the third
                                          quarter percentage change in the national Consumer Price
                                          Index (CPI) published by the United States Department of
                                          Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics.

                                  (ii)    The executive director must designate a substitute index to
                                          be used as a reference for adjustments if the CPI becomes
                                          unavailable.

D.     The definition of “Large Load Customer” should be adjusted to only identify
       expansions that will have a significant impact on the transmission system.
       Currently, the Second Discussion Draft subjects small, incremental expansions at existing
sites to this rulemaking, despite the fact that loads below 75 MW do not have a significant impact
on the transmission system. As discussed in the Workshop, it does not make sense to apply the
same financial obligations or interconnection studies to existing sites that are only adding 10 MW.
Critically, ERCOT set 75 MW as the impact threshold for new load, and only modifications that
increase the aggregate peak demand of a facility by 75 MW or more have to go through the large
load interconnection study process. 4 Loads below 75 MW are not driving forecast uncertainty and
do not impact the transmission system at the same level. To avoid subjecting small expansions to
this rule, the Commission should consider defining “Large Load Customer” as a customer that
adds 75 MW or more within a three-year period. Three years is a long enough timeframe that

       4
           ERCOT Planning Guide, Section 9.2.1(1)(b).


                                                        9
 ERCOT can accurately incorporate the impact of the existing site in its transmission planning
analysis. Further, high load factor customers prioritize speed to market, so it is unlikely any loads
would stand to benefit by developing a site in small increments over a longer period of time.

       To capture this approach, TIEC has provided updated language to the definition of Large
Load Customer in § (b)(9):

               (9)     Large load customer – A customer requesting a new or expanded
                       interconnection where the customer’s total peak demand at a single site is
                       equal to or exceeds will increase by at least 75 megawatts (MW) within a
                       three-year period.

                                      III.   CONCLUSION

       TIEC appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Second Discussion Draft and looks
forward to discussing the issues more in the future.

                                             Respectfully submitted,

C.     The generic intermediate security amount should be reduced and should take into
       account any security provided for significant equipment or services procured prior
       to executing an interconnection agreement.
       Under the Second Discussion Draft, the $/MW security associated with the Intermediate
Agreement is $100,000/MW, which is significantly higher than typical security and CIAC
requirements in a final service agreement.     This level of a security requirement, even if it is
ultimately refunded, may deter desirable and legitimate economic activity-particularly from cost-
sensitive industrial businesses competing in global markets. While this security will only be held
until a final service agreement is executed, that process can take a year or more today, and it is
uncertain what the process will look like if "batching" is implemented. The $/MW security is


                                                 6
 meant to act as a proxy for the costs of a final service agreement to determine whether a load is
"real" during the study process. As CenterPoint highlighted during the Workshop, applying the
$100,000/MW security requirement to a 2.5 GW customer load it is studying would amount to
$250 million-far exceeding the actual interconnection costs, which CenterPoint estimated to be
in the tens of millions.1 This demonstrates that such a high upfront generic security amount not
only unnecessarily ties up a large load customer's capital/credit, but also does little to verify the
legitimacy of the proposed load. In light of stakeholder feedback, TIEC recommends reducing the
security requirement to $20,000/MW to better reflect the actual purpose of the security amount.
For a large load, this amount would still be at least $1.5 million for a 75 MW load, instead of the
Second Discussion Draft's $7.5 million.

        Alternatively, TIEC re-urges its prior suggestion to adopt a tiered $/MW security amount
based on load size, similar to the distinction for the large load study fee. For example, a large load
customer with requested peak demand that is equal to 75 MW and less than 250 MW would be
subj ect to a $20,000/MW security requirement, while a large load customer with requested peak
demand that is equal to or greater than 250 MW would be required to pay $50,000/MW. Both
tiers provide sufficient security to ensure that the load is legitimate and committed, while also
aligning more closely with actual costs. This approach ensures that the security requirement is
proportionate to the scale ofthe load, promoting fairness and still protecting ratepayers and system
reliability.

        In addition, the $/MW security should recognize that a utility may request security for
certain long-lead time equipment prior to executing an interconnection agreement, and any security
provided for such equipment should count towards the $/MW requirement. Notably, the current

equipment at any stage ofthe ofthe interconnection process. Critically, Staff's Second Discussion
Draft only requires utilities to obtain financial security for any significant equipment or services
once an interconnection agreement is signed. However, there is nothing to prohibit a utility from
executing a Discretionary Services Agreement (DSA) or some other interim agreement and

D.     The definition of "Large Load Customer" should be adjusted to only identify
       expansions that will have a significant impact on the transmission system.
       Currently, the Second Discussion Draft subjects small, incremental expansions at existing
sites to this rulemaking, despite the fact that loads below 75 MW do not have a significant impact
on the transmission system. As discussed in the Workshop, it does not make sense to apply the
same financial obligations or interconnection studies to existing sites that are only adding 10 MW.
Critically, ERCOT set 75 MW as the impact threshold for new load, and only modifications that
increase the aggregate peak demand of a facility by 75 MW or more have to go through the large
load interconnection study process.4 Loads below 75 MW are not driving forecast uncertainty and
do not impact the transmission system at the same level. To avoid subjecting small expansions to
this rule, the Commission should consider defining "Large Load Customer" as a customer that
adds 75 MW or more within a three-year period. Three years is a long enough timeframe that

 •   Consistent with stakeholder feedback at the Workshop, the CIAC language should be
     adjusted to capture costs that are incurred solely to serve a large load customer, and system
     costs should not be part of the CIAC payment. Specifically, the language in subsection

     the interconnecting large load customer. This standard does not work.

     appropriately contribute to system costs, the Commission could consider a minimum
     demand charge for particularly large loads who are likely to justify significant transmission
     upgrades (for example, greater than 200 MW) for a limited period to ensure that the loads
     are paying for transmission. This type of a construct or other alternatives that protect
     ratepayers from stranded transmission costs could be considered in Project No. 58484.
 •   The Commission should give large loads flexibility in meeting their CIAC obligations with
     cash, corporate or parental guarantees, or letters of credit. Allowing these options provides
     utilities with protection while giving large loads additional flexibility.

     any security provided for significant equipment or services procured prior to executing an
     interconnection agreement.

     "Large Load Customef' as a customer that adds 75 MW or more within a three-year period.

     of the existing site in its transmission planning analysis. Further, high load factor
